archetype.name: Playoff Team (goalie-propped)
archetype.definition: Montreal is a team whose 5-on-5 play is finally a little above break-even, but whose spot near the top of the Atlantic rests on elite goaltending from Jacob Fowler and a league-best haul of close-game points.

report.headline: Real progress at 5-on-5, but Fowler and close games inflate the standings
report.take:
This is the fifth step of a steady climb. The Canadiens went from 55 points to 68, 76, 91 and then 106 last season, and they are now on a 109-point pace at 14-6-4. What is new is underneath the record. Every recent season in the sheet had Montreal losing the 5-on-5 chance battle, including last year's 106-point team at a 47.9% xGF. This year they sit at 50.7% xGF and 51% CF, eighth in the league in shot share. That is a modest edge, but it is the first time this group has been on the right side of the puck rather than surviving on top of it.

The record still runs well ahead of that edge. A +6 goal differential ranks 13th, right where the site's Teams tab puts them, yet 32 standings points would be a top-tier total. The gap is explained by Pts vs Goal Diff, where their 3.4 leads the league, and by Jacob Fowler. Fowler has a .918 save % and 12.5 GSAx, third among 72 goalies, and his GSAx alone exceeds the team's 11.5. Behind him, Jakub Dobes sits at .864 and -4.3. Montreal is close to a different team depending on which goalie starts.

What the record hides is a broken power play. At 14.3% it ranks 31st, far below the league's 22.5% and a long way from last season's 23.1%. The team is level with the league in goals per game despite giving away that much on the man advantage, which suggests the 5-on-5 attack is carrying the load. A 102.1 5-on-5 PDO says part of that is hot finishing or saves. The skater-row finishing figures in this sheet appear to cover only part of the roster, so the 5-on-5 PDO is the safer read. Defensively the structure is good against the blue line, holding opposing defensemen to 0.18 points a game, second-fewest. Opposing centers, though, take 36% of the points scored against Montreal, against a league norm of 27.6%.

The trend has already turned. After an 8-5 October at 3.46 goals a game, November has been 5-5 at 2.9 each way. The last five games went 2-3-0 with only 2 goals a game, 1.21 below their season rate. This roster has outrun its goal differential in each of the last three seasons, so some of that may be real. Still, a 109-point pace built on a top-five goalie season and the league's most fortunate close-game ledger is a ceiling, not a forecast. Expect a playoff-caliber team that settles into a crowded Atlantic scrum, not one that runs away from it.

strengths.title: Fowler is an elite starter
strengths.body: Fowler's .918 save % and 12.5 GSAx rank him third of 72 goalies, and he has started most of the games. He is the main reason the team's goalies rank fifth in GSAx and the defense eighth in goals allowed a game. Elite GSAx seasons rarely hold at this rate, and the drop to Dobes (.864, -4.3 GSAx) means every backup start is a real risk.

strengths.title: Finally winning the 5-on-5 share
strengths.body: A 50.7% xGF and 51% CF (eighth) are modest numbers. Set against last season's 47.9% xGF, they mark the first time this rebuild has tilted the ice instead of riding goaltending through being out-chanced. Shot-share edges are the most stable thing a team builds, so this is the part of the season most likely to last.

strengths.title: Stingy kill and blue-line coverage
strengths.body: The penalty kill sits at 80.5%, 12th and above the league's 77.2%. Opposing defensemen are held to 0.18 points a game, second-fewest in the league. That suppression keeps the goals-against line respectable even when Fowler isn't stealing games.

concerns.title: A power play in free fall
concerns.body: At 14.3% the power play ranks 31st, well under the league's 22.5% and last season's 23.1%. A unit that good a year ago probably isn't this bad, so some bounce-back is likely. Until it comes, Montreal gives away a structural edge every night and leans even harder on 5-on-5 play and Fowler.

concerns.title: Standings ahead of the goals
concerns.body: Montreal leads the league in Pts vs Goal Diff at 3.4, while its goal differential per game ranks only 13th. A 102.1 5-on-5 PDO adds a further tailwind. This group has beaten its goal differential three seasons running (7 and 5.6 the last two), so a slice may be repeatable. The full margin almost never is.

concerns.title: The offense has gone quiet
concerns.body: The last five games produced 2 goals a game, 1.21 below the season rate, and a 2-3-0 record. Over the last ten the differential is flat at 29-29. With the power play also cold, the scoring that carried October has thinned. The listed depth centers, Kapanen and Beck, have four points each, so the support scoring isn't filling the gap.

trend.note: October was the high point (8-5, 3.46 goals a game). November has flattened to 5-5 at 2.9 goals each way, and the last five games (2-3-0, 2 goals a game) are the weakest stretch yet.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games, two contenders, and a power play needing life
weekAhead.body:
The week opens at home against Los Angeles, 29th on the site at 7-12-2. The Kings have a 69.1% penalty kill (29th), D-graded goaltending at -7.4 GSAx, and a -0.57 goal differential per game. If the slumping attack and the dead power play are going to wake up, this is the night. One wrinkle: LA has held opposing centers further under their averages than any team.

Then comes a three-game trip. Colorado (eighth on the site) has a +0.96 goal differential per game, the No. 2 offense and A-graded forwards, and beat Montreal 4-1 on Nov 14. Their -2.8 Pts vs Goal Diff says the Avalanche are better than 13-7-3. Vegas (fifth) brings a 27.3% power play and an A-graded blue line. Utah closes the week with the league's second-best xGF % (56.8%) and a 32.5% power play, but also a 71.3% kill and goaltending at -10.3 GSAx, 30th. Montreal beat Utah 5-4 in overtime earlier this month. Coming out of this stretch at .500 would be a fair result.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs. two leaky kills
keyMatchups.body: Montreal's 14.3% power play gets the Kings' 69.1% kill and Utah's 71.3%, both bottom-six units. If the man advantage can't convert against these two, the problem is deeper than bad luck.

keyMatchups.title: Colorado's attack in Denver
keyMatchups.body: The Avalanche score at the league's second-best rate behind A-graded forwards and own a +0.96 goal differential per game. Their last visit from Montreal ended 1-4. This is the game where Fowler's form matters most.

keyMatchups.title: Kill vs. Vegas and Utah power plays
keyMatchups.body: Montreal's 80.5% kill faces the fourth-best (Vegas, 27.3%) and third-best (Utah, 32.5%) power plays on back-to-back stops. Staying out of the box matters more than usual on this trip.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the power play finally cashes in against the weak Los Angeles and Utah penalty kills. If it can't, the attack has nowhere to hide on the road.

restOfSeason.body:
The 109-point pace is the ceiling. Montreal's shot share is real and should hold near break-even or slightly better, and the power play is too far below last season's level not to recover somewhat. Two things will fade: the league-leading close-game luck and some of Fowler's elite GSAx. A team with a mid-pack goal differential finishing near 106 points again would be unusual. Our range is 95 to 102 points and 42 to 46 wins, playoff-caliber in a division where Tampa Bay, Ottawa, Boston and Florida are all bunched within a few points.

The biggest swing is in net. Fowler holding even a .910 level keeps Montreal safely in the top three of the Atlantic. A heavier Dobes workload at his current .864 would push them into the wild-card fight. A power play climbing back toward 18-19% would add some of the cushion the luck is about to take away.
swingFactors: Fowler sustaining elite GSAx and his share of starts
Power play recovering toward last season's level
How much of the close-game luck reverses

confidence.note: 24 games is enough for shot-share signals, but goaltending and close-game luck are volatile, and the roster section lists only two depth centers.
